What do FEOL, MOL and BEOL build?
column2: FEOL: the transistors in and on the silicon (isolation, wells, gate stack, source and drain), with the hottest steps. MOL: silicide, contacts and local interconnect to the first metal. BEOL: the copper/low-k wiring stack above, processed at about 400 °C or below.

column1: What is the Deal–Grove model, and when is oxide growth linear or parabolic?
column2: \(x^2 + Ax = B(t + \tau)\) from a flux balance of gas transport, diffusion through the oxide and reaction at the interface. Thin oxide (\(x \ll A\)) grows linearly at rate \(B/A\) (reaction-limited); thick oxide grows as \(\sqrt{Bt}\) (diffusion-limited). The two terms of \(t = x^2/B + x/(B/A)\) are equal at \(x = A\).

column1: How much silicon does thermal oxidation consume, and why?
column2: 0.44 of the oxide thickness: the ratio of silicon atoms per volume in SiO₂ (about 2.2 × 10²² cm⁻³) to that in silicon (5.0 × 10²² cm⁻³). 44% of the oxide lies below the original surface.

column1: Why is a modern gate built 'gate-last' (replacement metal gate)?
column2: A sacrificial polysilicon gate survives the hot source/drain steps and is then replaced by high-k dielectric, work-function metals and fill metal, which could not survive those temperatures. The liners eat the trench: \(w_{fill} = L_t - 2(t_{hk} + t_{wf})\).

column1: Why is copper wiring made by dual damascene?
column2: Copper cannot be plasma-etched, so trenches and vias are etched into the dielectric, lined with a barrier and seed, electroplated full of copper and polished back by CMP.

column1: Why do metal stacks have tiers of different thickness?
column2: A distributed wire's 50% delay is \(0.379RC \propto L^2/s^2\) when width and spacing scale by \(s\). Thin, dense local layers serve short connections; thick, wide upper layers carry long routes, clocks and power.

column1: How does contact resistance hurt a transistor?
column2: \(R_c = \rho_c/A_c\) rises as contacts shrink; in the source it degenerates the device, \(I_D' = I_D/(1 + g_mR_S)\). At advanced nodes MOL resistance is a major share of the parasitics.

column1: What does Little's law say about a fab, and what is DPML?
column2: WIP = start rate × cycle time, so 100,000 wafers a month with a 12-week (2.76-month) cycle means 2.76 × 10⁵ wafers in process (Example 25-01.7). Days per mask layer (roughly 1–1.5 [R-020]) times mask count gives the cycle time; long cycles tie up inventory and slow yield learning.

column1: What is the minimum pitch with on-axis and off-axis illumination?
column2: Imaging needs the zeroth and at least one first diffraction order inside the pupil. On-axis: \(p_{min} = \lambda/\text{NA}\). Off-axis, with the two orders at opposite pupil edges: \(\lambda/(2\text{NA})\), a half-pitch \(k_1\lambda/\text{NA}\) with \(k_1 \ge 0.25\).

column1: How does depth of focus scale with NA?
column2: DOF \(\approx n\lambda/\text{NA}^2\), twice the allowed defocus \(n\lambda/(2\text{NA}^2)\), so it shrinks faster than resolution improves: going from NA 0.33 to 0.55 cuts it by \((0.55/0.33)^2 \approx 2.8\).

column1: Why is EUV photon-starved?
column2: A 13.5 nm photon carries 91.8 eV against 6.42 eV at 193 nm, 14 times more, so the same dose delivers 14 times fewer photons. Relative shot noise \(1/\sqrt N\) then roughens edges and causes stochastic defects (missing contacts, bridges).

column1: How do dose and throughput trade in a scanner?
column2: wph \(= 3600\ \text{s}/(t_{oh} + t_{exp})\) with \(t_{exp} \propto D/P\). Raising dose to cut shot noise lengthens exposure and lowers throughput unless source power \(P\) rises.

column1: What are LELE and SADP/SAQP, and what does each cost?
column2: LELE splits a layer into two interleaved exposures and etches: half the pitch, but a second mask and overlay error between the sets. SADP/SAQP use sidewall spacers on a mandrel to halve or quarter the pitch without a second critical exposure, at the cost of more deposition and etch steps and pitch walk (spaces differing by \(2\delta\) for a mandrel error \(\delta\)).

column1: What is OPC?
column2: Optical proximity correction: deliberately distorting mask shapes (serifs, hammerheads, sub-resolution assist features) so that the printed pattern matches the design despite diffraction.

column1: What does High-NA EUV change?
column2: NA 0.55 instead of 0.33 resolves about 8 nm in one exposure, but its anamorphic optics halve the field to 26 mm × 16.5 mm (large dies need stitching), depth of focus falls and the tool costs about twice as much (reported prices; ASML lists none) [R-560], [R-561], [R-564].

column1: How is lithography cost per exposure pass estimated?
column2: \(c_{pass} = \text{price}/(\text{years} \times 8766\ \text{h} \times \text{availability} \times \text{wph})\): tool depreciation spread over the wafers it exposes. Each extra pass in multipatterning adds this and the steps around it.

column1: What limits a CVD deposition rate?
column2: \(v = [k_sh_g/(k_s + h_g)]\,C_g/N\), the series combination of surface reaction \(k_s\) and gas transport \(h_g\). Reaction-limited (\(k_s \ll h_g\)): uniform but temperature-sensitive. Transport-limited (\(h_g \ll k_s\)): fast but sensitive to gas flow and geometry.

column1: What makes ALD special?
column2: Alternating self-limiting half-reactions separated by purges add a fixed thickness per cycle (\(t = n_{cycles} \times\) GPC), giving near-perfect conformality and control on high-aspect-ratio structures at the cost of speed.

column1: Why is PVD used for barriers and seeds but not for filling deep features?
column2: Sputtered atoms arrive line-of-sight, so deposition is fast but step coverage falls with aspect ratio; thin liners are fine, deep fills are not.

column1: What are etch selectivity and anisotropy?
column2: Selectivity is the ratio of the film's etch rate to the stop layer's or mask's, setting how much of them an overetch consumes. Anisotropy (vertical faster than lateral) comes from directional ion bombardment and sidewall passivation in plasmas; wet etching is isotropic.

column1: What is Preston's equation, and what are dishing and erosion?
column2: CMP removal rate \(RR = K_pPv\): raised features carry more pressure and polish faster. Dishing recesses wide soft-metal lines; erosion thins the dielectric in dense arrays. Both depend on pattern density, hence dummy-fill rules.

column1: What is the as-implanted profile, and where is the junction?
column2: Approximately Gaussian about the projected range: \(N_p = Q/(\sqrt{2\pi}\Delta R_p)\), junction at \(x_j = R_p + \Delta R_p\sqrt{2\ln(N_p/N_B)}\) in background \(N_B\).

column1: What does an anneal do to an implant profile?
column2: It broadens the Gaussian while conserving dose: \(\Delta R_p'^2 = \Delta R_p^2 + 2Dt\), \(N_p' = N_p\Delta R_p/\Delta R_p'\). Every later hot step adds to the thermal budget.

column1: How do you judge whether a gauge is good enough?
column2: Measurement noise adds in quadrature, \(\sigma_{obs} = \sqrt{\sigma_p^2 + \sigma_m^2}\). The precision-to-tolerance ratio \(P/T = 6\sigma_m/(\text{USL} - \text{LSL})\) should be about 0.1 or less; above about 0.3 the gauge is inadequate.

column1: How many dies fit on a wafer?
column2: DPW \(\approx \pi d^2/(4A) - \pi d/\sqrt{2A}\): wafer area over die area, minus partial dies around the edge. A 100 mm² die gives about 640 on a 300 mm wafer by the formula; exact counts depend on grid placement and edge exclusion.

column1: What is the Poisson yield model and its key value?
column2: \(Y = e^{-AD_0}\), the probability of no killer defect when defects are independent and uniform. At \(AD_0 = 1\) (one defect per die on average) \(Y\) = 36.8%.

column1: Why do clustered defects give higher yield than Poisson?
column2: Yield is the Poisson yield averaged over the defect-density distribution, \(Y = \int e^{-AD}f(D)\,dD\), and since \(e^{-AD}\) is convex, spreading \(D\) raises the average (Jensen). Clustering wastes many defects on the same few dies.

column1: What are the negative-binomial and Murphy yield models?
column2: Negative binomial: \((1 + AD_0/\alpha)^{-\alpha}\), from a gamma-distributed \(D\); small \(\alpha\) means strong clustering and \(\alpha \to \infty\) gives Poisson. Murphy: \([(1 - e^{-AD_0})/AD_0]^2\), from a triangular \(D\).

column1: Why does cost per good die rise faster than die area?
column2: \(C_{die} = C_w/(\text{DPW} \times Y)\): a larger die gives fewer dies per wafer and each has a lower yield, so both factors work against it. This is the economic case for chiplets (25-07).

column1: What is core harvesting?
column2: Selling dies with a defective core disabled as a lower tier. With one spare among \(n\) cores, sellable yield is \(y_u[y_c^n + ny_c^{n-1}(1 - y_c)]\), much higher than all-good yield for large dies.

column1: How is yield learning modelled?
column2: \(D_0(t) = D_\infty + (D_{start} - D_\infty)e^{-t/\tau}\): defect density falls toward a mature floor as sources are found and fixed. Fast learning (short cycle times, good wafer maps) is a competitive advantage.

column1: Why might cost per transistor stop falling?
column2: \(C_{transistor} \propto C_w/(\text{density} \times Y)\): it falls only if density gains outpace wafer-price increases at comparable yield. Whether that still holds at recent nodes is contested.

column1: What is a PDK?
column2: A process design kit: the foundry's device models and corners, design rules and DRC/LVS/extraction decks, parameterized cells and libraries that let a design be built and signed off for one process.

column1: What is a PVT corner, and how does a threshold corner change delay?
column2: A combination of process, voltage and temperature at which timing and power are checked. With delay \(\propto V/(V - V_{TH})^\alpha\), a ±40 mV \(V_{TH}\) shift moves delay more at low supply, which is why low-voltage designs carry wide corners.

column1: What is FD-SOI back-gate biasing?
column2: A bias under the buried oxide shifts the threshold through a capacitive divider, \(\Delta V_{TH}/\Delta V_{BG} = -C_{Si}C_{BOX}/[C_{ox}(C_{Si} + C_{BOX})]\): tens of mV per volt, rising as the BOX thins. It trades speed against leakage after fabrication.

column1: What is an MPW shuttle?
column2: A multi-project wafer run in which many designs share one mask set, each buying area (cost \(\max(A, A_{min}) \times p_{mm^2}\)). Prototypes then cost tens of thousands rather than millions, at the price of schedule and few dies.

column1: What is a BCD process?
column2: Bipolar-CMOS-DMOS: logic, precision analog and high-voltage LDMOS on one die, used for power management, motor drivers and battery management.

column1: Why does a mixed-signal die gain less from a node shrink than a digital one?
column2: Logic area scales with density, but analog, I/O and passives are sized by matching, noise, voltage and inductor or capacitor values, which barely shrink, while wafer cost rises. The analog portion gets more expensive per function.

column1: Who dominated foundry revenue in 2Q26?
column2: TSMC, with about $40.2 B: 72.5% of the foundry market in TrendForce's count, or 75.2% of the top ten's $53.49 B; Samsung 5.9% and SMIC 5.4% of the market [R-578, as of Sep 2026].

column1: What is embedded NVM, and why does it matter for MCUs?
column2: Non-volatile memory (flash, or newer MRAM, RRAM or PCM) built on the logic die, so a microcontroller or secure element stores code and data without a separate chip. Foundries qualify each option separately; TSMC reports its 16 nm MRAM and 22ULL RRAM passed Automotive Grade 1 in 2025 [R-580].

column1: Wire bonding against flip-chip?
column2: Wire bonds are cheap and flexible but limited to the die perimeter and add about 1 nH per mm. Flip-chip spreads bumps over the whole die area, giving area-array I/O, short low-inductance paths and many power and ground connections.

column1: When does an area array beat perimeter pads?
column2: Perimeter pads give \(N \approx 4D/p_w\), an area array \((D/p_a)^2\); the array wins for die side \(D > 4p_a^2/p_w\). At 150 µm array pitch and 60 µm pad pitch the crossover is 1.5 mm (Example 25-06.1).

column1: What sets substrate layer count in escape routing?
column2: The traces between adjacent pads, \(n = \lfloor(p - d - s)/(w + s)\rfloor\), let each layer escape \(n + 1\) rows, so \(R\) rows need \(\lceil R/(n + 1)\rceil\) layers. Finer lines save layers and cost.

column1: What strains a solder joint, and which joints fail first?
column2: CTE mismatch: \(\gamma \approx \Delta\alpha\,\Delta T\,L_{DNP}/h\). Strain grows with distance from the neutral point, so corner joints fail first; taller joints help.

column1: What does the Coffin–Manson relation predict?
column2: Cycles to failure \(N_f \propto \gamma^{-n}\) with \(n \approx 2\) for solder: halving the strain roughly quadruples the life.

column1: What does underfill do?
column2: Epoxy between die and substrate bonds them so the mismatch strain is shared by the whole interface rather than concentrated in the solder joints, multiplying fatigue life.

column1: How does a package's life scale with its number of joints?
column2: Weakest link with a common Weibull shape \(\beta\): \(\eta_{pkg} = (\sum\eta_i^{-\beta})^{-1/\beta}\), and \(N\) identical joints give \(\eta N^{-1/\beta}\). 100 joints at \(\beta\) = 4 cut the life to \(100^{-1/4} \approx 0.32\) of one joint's.

column1: What are FOWLP, SiP and PoP?
column2: Fan-out wafer-level packaging embeds dies in a moulded wafer and builds thin RDL over it (no laminate substrate). System-in-package puts a whole subsystem (dies and passives) in one package. Package-on-package stacks memory on a processor package to save board area.

column1: What are 2.5D and 3D integration?
column2: 2.5D: dies side by side on wiring much finer than a substrate (silicon or RDL interposer, or silicon bridges such as EMIB or LSI). 3D: dies stacked and connected vertically by TSVs, microbumps or hybrid bonds, densest but hardest to cool and test.

column1: How does hybrid-bond density scale, and what limits pitch?
column2: \(n_{bond} = 1/p^2\): 10⁶/mm² at 1 µm, 10⁴/mm² at 10 µm. Overlay must stay within about \(p/4\) per axis, so placement accuracy, not lithography, limits pitch. Microbumps stop near 25 µm.

column1: What is die bond yield under Gaussian placement error?
column2: \(Y_{bond} = [\operatorname{erf}(p/(4\sigma\sqrt2))]^2\) for pads half the pitch wide and error \(\sigma\) per axis; it is about 91% at \(\sigma = p/8\) and 47% at \(p/4\), so placement error must stay well below \(p/8\).

column1: Die-to-wafer against wafer-to-wafer bonding?
column2: W2W reaches the finest overlay and pitch but bonds every die to whatever lies opposite, good or bad. D2W places tested known-good dies, allowing different die sizes, at coarser placement accuracy.

column1: Why do test escapes matter so much in chiplet packages?
column2: The escape rate among passing dies is \((1 - Y)(1 - c)/[Y + (1 - Y)(1 - c)]\), and one bad die scraps a package worth all the others: \(Y_{pkg} = y_a^n\prod(1 - e_i)\). Known-good die is the economic core of chiplets.

column1: When do chiplets beat a monolithic die on cost?
column2: When the yield gain from smaller dies exceeds the added test, packaging and attach losses: \(C = [\sum(cA_i + t)/Y_i + P]/y_a^n\). The gain is large for big dies at high \(D_0\) and shrinks as the process matures.

column1: What sets the anneal needed in hybrid bonding?
column2: Copper pads are recessed slightly below the oxide; on annealing, copper's higher expansion closes the gap: \(\Delta T_{close} = \delta/[(\alpha_{Cu} - \alpha_d)t]\), with copper about 17 ppm/K and oxide about 0.5 ppm/K.

column1: How big are CoWoS interposers now, and where are they going?
column2: In volume at 5.5 times the reticle with up to 12 HBM stacks; TSMC's roadmap shows 9.5 times in 2027 and 14 times in 2028 [R-587, as of Apr 2026].

column1: How is a junction temperature budget built?
column2: Heat flows through series resistances: \(T_J = T_{fluid} + P\sum R_i\), with slabs \(R = t/(kA)\) and convection \(R = 1/(hA)\). At 1,000 W, every 0.01 K/W costs 10 K.

column1: Why are TIMs a major resistance despite being thin?
column2: Their conductivity is only a few W/(m·K) against 150 for silicon and 400 for copper, so a 25 µm layer at 5 W/(m·K) over 800 mm² adds 0.00625 K/W, as much as a 2 mm copper lid (Example 25-08.1).

column1: What is spreading resistance?
column2: The extra resistance when heat from a small source must spread sideways. A uniform-flux disk of radius \(a\) on a large block has centre rise \(qa/k\) and average resistance \(8/(3\pi^2ka) \approx 0.27/(ka)\); it dominates for hotspots.

column1: What is fin efficiency?
column2: The heat a fin removes over what it would remove at base temperature everywhere: \(\eta_f = \tanh(mL)/(mL)\), \(m = \sqrt{2h/(kt_f)}\). Making fins longer than \(mL \approx 1\)–2 adds little.

column1: Why does liquid cooling win at kilowatt power?
column2: Water holds about 3,470 times the heat per volume of air, and forced-liquid \(h\) is far higher, so the fluid rise \(P/(\rho\dot Vc_p)\) and convection resistance both fall. The junction sits near \(T_{in} + \Delta T_{fluid}/2 + P\sum R\).

column1: What are a vapor chamber, a cold plate and immersion cooling?
column2: Vapor chamber: a sealed flat chamber that spreads heat by evaporation and condensation, far better than solid copper. Cold plate: a channelled metal block carrying pumped coolant, the standard for kilowatt accelerators. Immersion: servers submerged in dielectric liquid, single- or two-phase, still a niche.

column1: Why does the hottest part of a mission profile dominate wear-out?
column2: Damage is roughly Arrhenius, so the equivalent temperature \(T_{eq} = -E_a/\{k\ln[\sum w_ie^{-E_a/kT_i}]\}\) sits well above the time-average: a few hot hours outweigh many cool ones.

column1: Why must TDP numbers be compared with care?
column2: Vendors define them differently (per-GPU TDP, typical board power, configurable limits), so boundaries must be checked. AI accelerators reached 1–1.4 kW in 2024–2025 with roadmaps toward 2 kW and more [R-596–R-598].

column1: What is an Arrhenius acceleration factor?
column2: \(AF_T = \exp[(E_a/k)(1/T_{use} - 1/T_{stress})]\), temperatures in kelvin. Each mechanism has its own \(E_a\), and because the dependence is exponential an error of 0.1 eV shifts the factor between a 300 °C test and 105 °C use by about 2.8 times.

column1: What is Black's equation?
column2: \(MTTF = Aj^{-n}e^{E_a/kT}\) for electromigration. \(n \approx 2\) when void nucleation dominates, \(\approx 1\) when growth dominates (observed about 1–3); copper along its cap interface has \(E_a \approx 0.9\) eV.

column1: Why does a measured EM current exponent depend on the test current?
column2: With \(MTTF = Bj^{-2} + Cj^{-1}\), the local exponent is \(n = (2 + x)/(1 + x)\), \(x = j/j^*\): near 2 at low current, near 1 at high. A high-current test can understate the exponent at use conditions.

column1: What is the Blech effect?
column2: Back-stress from atoms piling up at a line's end opposes the electron wind; if \(jL < (jL)_c = \Omega\Delta\sigma_c/(Z^*e\rho)\) the flux stops and the line is immortal to EM. Short lines can carry more current.

column1: Why do the E, 1/E and power-law TDDB models disagree?
column2: All fit stress data over a narrow high-field range, but they extrapolate differently to use fields, by many orders of magnitude. The E model (\(t \propto e^{-\gamma E}\)) predicts the shortest life and is the conservative choice; which is right is contested.

column1: How does Weibull area scaling affect oxide reliability?
column2: A chip with \(A_{chip}/A_{test}\) times the area fails sooner: \(t_F = \eta_{test}(A_{chip}/A_{test})^{-1/\beta}[-\ln(1 - F)]^{1/\beta}\). Low \(\beta\) (thin oxides) makes the penalty severe.

column1: What are BTI and HCI?
column2: BTI: a partly recoverable threshold shift under gate bias at temperature (NBTI in PMOS, PBTI in NMOS), roughly \(\Delta V_{TH} = At^{n_t}\). HCI: damage from carriers accelerated near the drain. Both slow circuits over life and are covered by aging guard bands.

column1: How is a FIT bound derived from an HTOL test?
column2: \(\lambda_U = \chi^2_{CL,2f+2}/(2NtAF)\) for \(f\) failures in \(N\) units × \(t\) hours at acceleration \(AF\); 60% confidence is common in supplier reliability reports [R-610]. Zero failures still give a nonzero bound set by device-hours.

column1: What does qualification prove, and what does it not?
column2: A standard set of accelerated stresses (HTOL, temperature cycling, humidity, ESD, latch-up) shows no gross reliability weakness. On its own it does not demonstrate a field failure rate; that needs acceleration models and device-hours.

column1: What are AEC-Q100 temperature grades?
column2: Ambient operating ranges: Grade 0 −40 to +150 °C, Grade 1 −40 to +125 °C, Grade 2 −40 to +105 °C, Grade 3 −40 to +85 °C [R-612, Rev J, Aug 2023].

column1: How is a temperature-cycling test converted to field life?
column2: Coffin–Manson: \(AF_{TC} = (\Delta T_s/\Delta T_{field})^n\) with \(n \approx 2\) for solder; field cycles = test cycles × AF, divided by field cycles per year.

column1: What is an ASIL?
column2: An Automotive Safety Integrity Level, A (least) to D (most demanding), assigned to a safety goal from the severity, exposure and controllability of the hazard. A chip supports ASIL D goals; it is not itself 'ASIL D'.

column1: What are SPFM and LFM?
column2: SPFM \(= 1 - \sum(\lambda_{SPF} + \lambda_{RF})/\sum\lambda\), coverage of single-point and residual faults. LFM \(= 1 - \sum\lambda_{latent}/\sum(\lambda - \lambda_{SPF} - \lambda_{RF})\), coverage of latent faults. Targets for ASIL B/C/D: SPFM ≥ 90/97/99%, LFM ≥ 60/80/90%.

column1: What is PMHF?
column2: The average rate at which random hardware faults violate a safety goal: \(\approx \sum(\lambda_{SPF} + \lambda_{RF}) + \lambda_L\lambda_D\tau\). Targets: below 100 FIT for ASIL B and C, below 10 FIT for ASIL D.

column1: Why does a latent fault matter, and how is it controlled?
column2: A fault in a safety mechanism (for example a lockstep comparator) violates nothing until a second fault arrives; the dual-point term \(\lambda_L\lambda_D\tau\) grows with exposure time \(\tau\). Start-up or periodic self-tests shorten \(\tau\) and raise LFM.

column1: Why do automotive parts need ppm-level defect rates?
column2: A vehicle has about 10⁴ semiconductor components (one supplier's estimate is about 40 systems × 250 components [R-615]), so at a defect rate \(p\) per component the fraction of vehicles with at least one bad part is \(1 - (1 - p)^N \approx Np\): at 0.5 ppm each, 10⁴ components put a bad part in about 0.5% of vehicles.

column1: What does wafer sort do that final test cannot, and vice versa?
column2: Wafer sort probes every die before dicing, so bad dies are not packaged, and produces wafer maps for yield learning. Final test catches assembly damage and runs at temperature and speed to assign bins.

column1: How is test cost per good die computed?
column2: \(c_{test} = r(T_N + t_i)/N\) per die tested at cell rate \(r\), \(N\) sites and index time \(t_i\); per good die divide by yield, because bad dies take test time too.

column1: What is multisite efficiency?
column2: \(\eta = 1 - (T_N - T_1)/[(N - 1)T_1]\): the fraction of the ideal parallel speed-up achieved. Shared instruments and the slowest site lower it, so doubling sites rarely halves cost.

column1: How do guard bands trade escapes against overkill?
column2: With tester error, a part ships if its measured value clears the limit plus a guard band \(g\). Raising \(g\) cuts escapes (bad parts shipped) but increases overkill (good parts rejected) and pushes parts down speed bins; tester accuracy sets the price of the trade.

column1: How is speed-bin revenue computed?
column2: With Gaussian \(F_{max}\), each bin's fraction is \(\Phi((b - \mu)/\sigma) - \Phi((a - \mu)/\sigma)\), and revenue per die is the bin fractions weighted by their prices. A guard band a third of \(\sigma\) can cost about a tenth of revenue.

column1: How long must burn-in run?
column2: Long enough to age the weak subpopulation: \(AF\,t_b = \eta_w[\ln(p_w/q)]^{1/\beta}\) cuts a weak fraction \(p_w\) to \(q\). A shallow weak-population \(\beta\) needs much longer burn-in, and every hour costs capacity and power for every part.

column1: What are WLBI and SLT?
column2: Wafer-level burn-in stresses whole wafers so weak dies are removed before they consume a package or multi-die module. System-level test boots real software on an application-like board, catching timing-marginal defects that structural tests miss.

column1: How big is the cost of test, and is it rising?
column2: Historically about 2% of manufacturing cost; one venture estimate puts leading AI parts toward 5–7% of ASP [R-618, May 2026]. Two vendors, Advantest and Teradyne, hold about 90% or more of the ATE market by the same estimate.

column1: What is post-silicon validation, and how does it differ from manufacturing test?
column2: Validation asks whether the design is right on real silicon, running real software across voltage, frequency and temperature; manufacturing test asks whether each part was built right. Bugs found in validation lead to errata, workarounds or respins.

column1: What does bring-up involve?
column2: Taking first silicon from power-on through clocks, reset, debug access and boot to running real software, usually on a purpose-built validation board.

column1: Why is a trace buffer's window so short?
column2: Storage is signals × depth, and the window is depth divided by clock frequency: 4,096 entries at 2 GHz cover only about 2 µs. Signal selection and triggering decide what can be seen.

column1: What is a shmoo plot?
column2: A pass/fail map over two swept conditions, usually supply voltage and frequency; its boundary follows \(F_{max} = K(V - V_{TH})^\alpha/V\), and holes or bends point to marginal circuits. \(V_{min}\) is read off at the target frequency.

column1: What are a scan dump and a chicken bit?
column2: A scan dump stops the clocks and shifts out every scan flip-flop for a full snapshot of internal state. A chicken bit is a configuration bit designed in to disable or alter a feature, so a silicon bug can be worked around without a hardware fix.

column1: How does a reliability-growth model help decide 'are we done?'
column2: The Goel–Okumoto curve \(m(t) = a(1 - e^{-bt})\) fitted to bug counts estimates the total \(a\), the bugs remaining \(a - m(t)\) and the time to find a fraction \(q\), \(\ln[1/(1 - q)]/b\). It is crude, but it makes the question quantitative.

column1: How is a respin decision framed?
column2: As a decision tree: expected cost = Σ probability × (fix cost + delay cost) for each branch, such as a cheap metal-only fix that may fail against a full respin. The break-even success probability shows how confident the team must be.

column1: What does the 2026 first-silicon survey say, and how certain is it?
column2: 5% of 320 IC/ASIC respondents reported first-silicon success (14% in 2024) [R-621, R-622]. The 95% Wilson interval is about 3–8%, and a 2024 change in recruitment method confounds the trend.
